judgments.reasoning_cat1: The insuring clause is the standard promise to pay death proceeds to the beneficiary on due proof of death while the contract was in force; 'due proof' and 'in force' are settled insurance terms rather than genuinely ambiguous ones.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is expressly made 'subject to its terms', which harmonises it with the Suicide (c034), Incontestability (c033) and Grace Period (c023) provisions, so no free-standing conflict appears.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A 20-day unconditional cancellation right with a premium refund is a simple mechanic; the surviving words name a definite period and a definite consequence.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It sits directly against the 'Notice to Policyholder — Right to Return Policy' pages (c004, c005, c006), which give 30 or 45 days where the policy replaces an existing policy, so the free-look period a replacement purchaser actually has is not settled by this clause alone.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The surviving text is only a list of state abbreviations with the operative return right missing, so on its face it states no rule at all and the enumeration invites an expressio unius reading against unlisted states.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is one of a set of state-specific free-look provisions (c004-c006) that all differ from the 20-day right in c002, so the interaction of the general and state riders is genuinely open.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The condition 'if this life insurance policy replaces an existing policy' is the trigger, and what counts as 'replaces' is the kind of term parties fight over; the surviving text is also scrambled so the 30-day right and its condition run together.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It gives a longer return period than the general 20-day right in c002 and applies only to enumerated states, leaving its relationship to c002 and to the PA provision (c006) unresolved.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The California version repeats the same 'replaces an existing policy' trigger and 30-day return right in capitals; the term 'replaces' carries the same latent uncertainty, though the rule itself is plain.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It conflicts on its face with the 20-day cancellation right in c002 for a California policy, but this policy was not issued in California, which limits the practical tension.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The Pennsylvania paragraph is the most badly mangled of the set, giving a 45-day period tied to a condition ('if we issue your ... policy') that cannot be read off the words, which is a mechanical defect that changes meaning.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It states a period different from both c002 (20 days) and c004/c005 (30 days), and the policy is a replacement-policy dispute, so the fit of this state rider with the general cancellation right is squarely in play.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A footnote saying premiums are affected by risk class and that no one is authorised to represent future changes; the words are scrambled but the message is a plain disclaimer.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It matches the identical footnotes at c008 and c014 and the Risk Class definition (c021), so it fits the instrument.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Duplicate risk-class footnote on the continued specifications page; a boilerplate disclaimer with no term requiring construction.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is verbatim consistent with c007 and c014 and with the Conversion-Premium clause (c051) on risk class, so no relational defect appears.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A table legend stating installments are monthly and per $1,000 of proceeds applied; definite and arithmetic.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is consistent with the option descriptions (c037-c045) and the actuarial basis note (c013).

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A definitional legend that 'age' means age nearest birthday; the OCR has destroyed the defined word, but the intended rule is a single conventional measure.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It aligns with the life-income options which are 'based on the payee's sex and age' (c037), so it supplies rather than contradicts a term.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A note that ages beyond the tables are available and rates will be furnished on request; 'upon request' is mechanical, not ambiguous.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is duplicated for Option 5 at c012 and consistent with the Alternate Life Income clause (c045).

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Same availability note directed at Option 5; plain and self-contained.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with c011 and with the Option 5 description at c043; no tension found.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: An actuarial basis statement identifying the mortality table, projection scale and a 3% interest rate; specific numbers, no ambiguous term.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The 3% basis here sits beside the 4.5% commutation rate in Death of Payee (c046) and the 'at least as liberal' alternate rates in c045, but those address different calculations and can be harmonised.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The third copy of the risk-class footnote, attached to the guaranteed maximum renewal premium table; a disclaimer with no operative uncertainty.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It coexists with the Renewal clause (c024) and the guaranteed maximum table, which together fix renewal premiums, so nothing contradicts it.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The contract-months-and-years definition survives only as a fragment, so how contract years are measured from the contract date cannot be read off the text as given.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Contract date (8/10/07) and issue date (8/1/07) differ on page 3, and the Incontestability and Suicide clauses (c033, c034) run from 'date of issue', so which date starts the two-year clocks is a live relational question.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'A notice takes effect when signed; but it is subject to any payment made or action taken by us before we receive it' creates a genuine tension between the effective date and the receipt date of a notice.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It bears on the Assignment clause (c027), which says no assignment binds the insurer 'unless we receive notice of it', so the signed-versus-received timing has to be reconciled across the two.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A one-line definition of 'option' as payment of proceeds other than in one sum; short but definite.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It matches the Payment of Proceeds clause (c031) and the option descriptions in c038-c045.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Payee' is defined as the person to whom payments are made and, for life income options, the person on whose life the option is based; the fragment blurs the two uses.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It interacts with c035 (payee must be the beneficiary if an option is chosen for death proceeds) and c036 (corporate payees), which can be harmonised.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The pronoun definition makes 'you' the insured but the owner when contract rights, payments and notices are concerned, a split reference that can genuinely be read two ways in a given clause.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The Accelerated Benefit Rider redefines the same pronouns (c059) and the rider-controls clause (c057) governs conflicts, so the two definitions have to be read together.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'The proof must be acceptable to us' is a discretionary standard whose boundary is not fixed, and the fragment about no new benefit amount taking effect until approval compounds it.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It supports the Reinstatement clause (c025) and the Conversion clause (c047), which waives insurability proof, and those fit rather than conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Only a stub survives ('Unless we adopt other rules, your risk ...'), so the definition of risk class is not stated; the 'unless we adopt other rules' carve-out is itself open-ended.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The risk-class footnotes (c007, c008, c014) say no one may represent future changes, which sits uneasily with an insurer reserving power to adopt other rules.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A fragmentary premium-payment clause requiring premiums after the first to be paid in advance of the period to which they apply; the rule is conventional.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It works with the Grace Period (c023), Renewal (c024) and the renewal premium table, and no inconsistency emerged.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The clause gives 31 days of grace yet says the contract ends 'as of the premium due date', a retroactive termination that reads oddly against the promise to give notice before the contract ends.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It must be reconciled with the insuring clause's requirement that death occur 'while the contract was in force' (c001) and with Reinstatement (c025); the deemed-lapse date is exactly where those meet.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Renewal by paying 'the premium then due', with no renewal past the final term date on page 3; simple and referenced to a specific page.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The renewal premium table (page 6) is captioned 'guaranteed maximum' while the specifications page says premiums are subject to change, so the amount 'then due' is fixed by other pages that do not perfectly agree.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The reinstatement conditions survive as a numbered list but the qualifying period, interest and evidence-of-insurability requirements are truncated, leaving the conditions incompletely stated.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Reinstatement bears directly on the two-year clocks in Incontestability (c033) and Suicide (c034) — whether they restart on reinstatement is not addressed anywhere.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Only a fragment of the Ownership provision survives, referring to rights in the Beneficiary and Proceeds Payment Options sections and to a revocable beneficiary or contingent owner; no operative rule is legible.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It cross-refers to c028 (Beneficiary) and c035 (choice of options by owner), which are themselves fragmentary, so the ownership/beneficiary interface is not fully worked out.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The clause conditions the insurer's recognition of an assignment on receiving notice and gives the assignee a 'first claim', but the surviving words do not say what the assignee's claim ranks against.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It has to be read with Beneficiary (c028) and Payment of Proceeds (c031) to know whether an assignee takes ahead of a named beneficiary, a classic point of interaction.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The beneficiary clause survives only in pieces — survivorship, rights within 'the same class', and what happens if no beneficiary survives — so the class and default rules are not legible.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It ties to Ownership (c026), Assignment (c027) and the requirement in c035 that a death-proceeds payee be the beneficiary, and those pieces must be harmonised.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: It says statements are representations 'true as far as you know and believe' and not warranted, yet also that no claim may be denied on a statement unless it is in an attached application; the interaction of the two limbs is a real construction point.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: This misrepresentation limit sits directly against the Incontestability clause (c033), which allows contest within two years, so the scope of permissible claim denial depends on reading both together.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Proceeds paid within 30 days after receipt of proof of death; a definite period keyed to a definite event.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It matches the insuring clause's 'due proof' trigger (c001) and the interest-on-proceeds clause (c032), so the timing scheme is coherent.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The surviving words say proceeds are paid in one sum unless an option is chosen, with a reserved 'we may ...' that is cut off; the reserved power cannot be measured from the text.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is the hinge between Claims (c030) and the Proceeds Payment Options (c035-c045) and is consistent with the definition of 'option' (c017).

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The interest rate is stated as 'at the rate of at l[east] ...% per year, but not less than that required by law', a floor stated twice by reference to an external standard, and the OCR loses the number entirely.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It has to be squared with the Option 1 interest rate (c038), which lets the insurer announce a higher rate, and with the 3% actuarial basis (c013).

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The incontestability text runs two clocks — two years after date of issue and two years after any increase or reinstatement — and reserves contest 'at any time' for non-payment; which amounts fall in which period is exactly the sort of division that is argued over.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It runs in parallel with the Suicide clause (c034) and the Conversion 'Incontestability and Suicide' clause (c055), and whether the periods restart on a replacement or converted policy is not resolved by any of them.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The suicide exclusion turns on 'suicide or intentional self-destruction, while sane or insane', a two-year period, and a limited return of premiums, and the surviving text ties the exclusion to 'amounts ... in effect for less than 2 years' — the ambiguity is which amounts, and from which date the two years run.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Read against Incontestability (c033), the Conversion incontestability-and-suicide clause (c055) and the replacement-policy return provisions (c004-c006), whether a replacement policy starts a fresh two-year suicide period or inherits the predecessor's is genuinely unsettled on this instrument.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: It requires that where an option is chosen for death proceeds, 'the payee, or one of the payees, must be the beneficiary', which is a definite condition even though the consent language around it is garbled.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It depends on the Beneficiary (c028) and Ownership (c026) provisions and on the definition of payee (c018); the requirement is consistent with those.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The enumerated payees (corporation, insured, spouse or child) are followed by a discretionary catch-all for 'anyone else related to the insured by blood or [marriage]' if the insurer agrees, a classic general-after-specific structure.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It restricts corporate payees to options 2 or 4 while the option descriptions (c038-c045) and Choice of Options (c035) contain no such limit, but the restriction reads as a carve-out rather than a contradiction.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The surviving text promises a supplementary contract showing the option terms and says life income options are 'based on the payee's sex and age'; only the fragment 'if you request and we approve' is open-ended.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is consistent with the settlement option tables and the age definition (c010), and with Alternate Life Income (c045).

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Option 1 preserves an insurer discretion to 'determine and announce a higher' interest rate and lists payment frequencies, but the guaranteed rate itself is lost from the text.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Almost nothing survives beyond the heading and a reference to a right to withdraw the proceeds, so no term can be identified as ambiguous.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It sits with the Option 2 table on page 5 and the Death of Payee commutation rule (c046), which expressly covers option 2, so it is accounted for elsewhere.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Only the first-payment timing and 'as long as the payee is living' survive; the guaranteed period variants are lost but the surviving rule is conventional.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It works with the option 3 tables (non-refund, 5/10/20 year guaranteed periods, installment refund at c041) and with Death of Payee (c046).

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The installment refund limb states a definite mechanic — equal monthly payments until the total equals the proceeds applied, then continued payments for life; nothing in it carries two readings.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It fits the Option 3 heading (c040), the option tables on page 5 and the commutation rule for option 3 in Death of Payee (c046).

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Only the tail survives — that the final payment equals the unpaid balance and there is a right to withdraw the proceeds — so no ambiguous term is identifiable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is consistent with Death of Payee (c046), which treats option 4 as leaving 'any balance held by us', and with the corporate payee limitation in c036.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The clause identifies a two-payee joint and survivor income keyed to the option 5 table on page 5; the surviving words are fragmentary but the rule is standard.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It cross-refers to the page 5 table and to the availability note (c012) and Alternate Life Income (c045), which match it.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The 'Joint and 2/3' variant says full payment while both payees live and a reduced payment after one dies, but the surviving text does not legibly state the two-thirds reduction it is named for.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It depends on the option 5 tables on page 5 (three separate rate grids), and which grid corresponds to this variant is not labelled in the surviving text.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Rates at least as liberal as those we then charge ... for a single premium immediate annuity of the same kind' is a comparative standard whose application to a given case is not self-executing.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It overrides the page 5 tables and interacts with Death of Payee (c046), which says the commutation rate will be separately specified when the alternate life income is chosen, so the two are drafted to fit.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The clause fixes a 4.5% commutation rate for options 2, 3 and 5 and a balance rule for options 1 and 4, then says the rate will be separately specified for alternate life income — specific numbers, with one reserved variable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The 4.5% commutation rate sits against the 3% actuarial basis of the tables (c013) and the Option 1 interest rate (c038), a difference that is intentional in annuity drafting but visible on the face of the instrument.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The core promise — conversion to a new contract without proving insurability — survives, but the conditions and time limits are lost, and 'may be converted' leaves the window unstated in this clause.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It depends on the Conversion Date (c048), Plan (c049), Amount (c050) and Notice (c052) clauses, which supply the missing limits, so the group is designed to be read together.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The clause says the conversion date 'may be any time' with the new contract effective at the later of the conversion date and premium payment, but the outer limit on 'any time' is missing from the surviving text.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It must be read with the Notice clause (c052), which requires a request within 31 days before the conversion date, and with Renewal's final term date (c024); those constrain a date the clause itself leaves open.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'The new contract may be any whole life plan that we [then issue]' turns on the insurer's own offering list, which is indefinite in the abstract but conventional in a conversion clause.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It fits the Amount (c050), Premium (c051) and If Disabled (c054) clauses, all of which assume a whole life plan.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Premium at 'our then published rates for such plan and your age at that time', with the risk class carried over; the pricing reference is external but definite in method.

judgments.reasoning_cat2: The 31-day request window narrows the 'any time' language in c048, and the two read together rather than contradict, though the interface is where a dispute would arise.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A dense list of rider restrictions with an open catch-all — 'You may only have other riders if we agree' — sitting after specific prohibitions on waiver-of-premium and accidental death riders, the classic general-after-specific structure.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It interacts with the Accelerated Benefit Rider attached here (c056-c073) and its termination clause (c073), and whether that rider carries over on conversion is not addressed.

judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is the express exception to the minimum-amount rule in c050 and refers back to 'the rider's terms', a waiver-of-premium rider not reproduced in this instrument.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Only the heading and the word 'contract' survive, so the rule on how the incontestability and suicide periods carry into a converted contract is entirely absent from the text as given.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: This is precisely the bridge between the Incontestability (c033) and Suicide (c034) clauses and a successor contract, and in a replacement-policy dispute whether the periods run afresh is the central relational question.

judgments.reasoning_cat2: It duplicates the premium-reduction rule at c072 and depends on the Contract Values formula (c070), which is itself only fragmentarily legible.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Where the rider and contract differ, the rider controls' is a short priority rule; its reach — whether it overrides every contract term or only rider-related ones — is not delimited.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is the express mechanism resolving clashes such as the competing pronoun definitions at c019 and c059, so it operates on the rest of the instrument by design.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The rider begins on the later of the contract effective date and (presumably) the rider's own date; the second limb is lost, leaving the start date incompletely stated.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It has to be squared with the contract date and issue date on page 3 and with the rider's qualifying requirement that the rider and contract be in effect (c062).

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The rider's pronoun definition, like the policy's, makes 'you' the insured except for contract rights, where it means the owner; the split creates a real risk of two readings in the rider's own clauses.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It duplicates c019 and matters because the rider pays 'the owner' (c061) while the qualifying requirements are framed around 'you' being diagnosed (c062), so the definitions must be traced through.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Physician' is defined by licensure plus exclusions of you, spouse, parent, child, sibling and household members — a closed and specific definition.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It supports the qualifying requirements (c062), the additional examination clause (c065) and the medical referee (c067), all consistent.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The benefit statement survives only in pieces, including a partly legible limit tied to having more than one contract with the insurer, so the maximum accelerable amount cannot be read off the words.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It works with the Contract Values formula (c070) and the qualifying requirement that payment not reduce the contract below the minimum issue limit (c062), which cap the same amount by different routes.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The list of cumulative requirements is legible in part, but the consent requirement for 'other persons having rights in the contract' is garbled and the diagnosis condition depends on 'terminal condition' as defined elsewhere.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It depends on the Terminal Condition definition (c063), the Physician definition (c060) and the minimum issue limit also used in c050, and those pieces fit.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Terminal condition' — a non-correctable condition that will with reasonable medical certainty result in death within a period stated in the physician's statement — is the single most litigated kind of definition in an accelerated benefit rider, and the survival period is illegible here.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is the trigger for c061, c062 and c064, so any uncertainty in it propagates through the rider, though nothing else in the instrument contradicts it.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Request for payment' means your written request accompanied by a physician's statement that you have a terminal condition; the surviving text is fragmentary but the definition is procedural.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It keys to the Terminal Condition definition (c063), the additional-proof clause (c065) and the interest rate timing in c071, which runs from the time payment is requested.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The clause reserves a right to require additional proof and examination by a physician of the insurer's choice at its expense; 'additional proof' is open-ended but the discretion is standard.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It leads directly into the medical referee procedure (c067) and the cost allocation (c068), which are consistent with it.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A recommendation to consult a tax advisor before adding the rider or requesting payment; hortatory rather than operative, so there is little to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Nothing else in the instrument bears on tax treatment, so no relational tension exists.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The referee mechanism is detailed — a disinterested third physician acceptable to both, whose decision the insurer will accept — and 'disinterested' and 'acceptable to both' are the only soft terms.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It follows from the additional-examination right (c065), uses the Physician definition (c060) and is completed by the cost clause (c068), so the sequence is coherent.

judgments.reasoning_cat2: It completes c067 and c065 and matches their allocation of expense to the insurer where the decision favours the insured.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Payment in a lump sum or, at the owner's choice, under any proceeds payment option 'except those which are contingent on the life of the insured' — a specific exclusion carved out of a general permission.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The exclusion knocks out options 3 and 5 (c040, c043) while leaving options 1, 2 and 4 available, which reads consistently with the option provisions.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The Contract Values formula survives only as disconnected fragments — 'A is the benefit paid under this rider', '$100', 'state where this rider is issued' — so the reduction calculation cannot be derived from the words at all.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is the operative computation behind c056, c061 and c072, all of which promise a reduction 'appropriate' to the accelerated benefit, so the missing formula is felt across the rider.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The interest rate is capped by the Moody's Composite Yield on Seasoned Corporate Bonds with a fallback to 'a substantially similar average acceptable to the state insurance commissioner', a defined but externally referenced ceiling with a soft fallback.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It sets a rate different in kind from the death-proceeds interest floor (c032) and the option interest rate (c038), but they govern different payments and can coexist.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Premiums reduce to the level required for the reduced death proceeds; the doubled 'will will' is a typographic slip that does not change meaning.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It restates the second sentence of c056 almost verbatim, a duplication that is redundant rather than contradictory, and it depends on the Contract Values formula (c070).

judgments.reasoning_cat2: It has to fit the Grace Period lapse rule (c023), the Reinstatement clause (c025) and the Conversion riders clause (c053), none of which says what becomes of this rider on lapse, reinstatement or conversion.
